sent_to_model:
I'm replying to someone online who's dealing with an abusive partner and is cut off from friends and family. There's also an issue with getting their house key back. I went through a four-year relationship like this, and their worry about being alone really got to me. Can you help me write a reply using my experience? I want them to understand why I believe it's abuse and why getting the key back isn't enough to feel safe. I also want to talk about getting support and how hard being alone was afterward, because things did eventually get better for me, but it took time. Please mention professional help, police accompaniment if exchanging property feels unsafe, and my hope that they learn to recognise abuse and never face it again.

- Relationship with abusive man lasted four years.
- Mother lived on the other side of the country; held several jobs.
- Recipient describes being separated from friends and relatives; unclear whether they have a therapist.
- Returning a house key doesn't rule out an extra copy existing.
- Writer attended therapy weekly after the breakup.
- Writer lost all their friends because the partner disapproved of them, citing even occasional drinking and insulting them sexually.
- Writer was attending university during the aftermath.
- Feared leaving because there would be nobody around. Weekly therapy became the only regular support afterward.
- Therapist and mother independently identified the relationship as abusive on the same day; mother spoke by phone.
- Those two people had never met; both cared about writer's welfare. Their agreement made the abuse harder to dismiss.
- After leaving, writer experienced severe distress, substantial weight loss and withdrawal from conversation.
- University work became the main focus during that period.
- Sometimes questioned leaving when both solitude and staying with the partner seemed equally unhappy.
- Eventually formed friendships and reached out to people from before the relationship.
- Recognizing the abuse was initially shocking.
- Having support again required learning how to accept and seek it.
- Eventually understood that life could offer something beyond unhappiness.
- Abuse has lasting effects; recovery can be slow and painful.
- Urge recipient to replace the locks, even if the key is returned.
- Mention possible police accompaniment for a property exchange when worried about safety; writer believes most departments offer this.
- Encourage professional help and rebuilding personal connections.
- Hope recipient gains awareness from the experience and avoids another abusive relationship.

(About me: abuse survivor who attended university during the aftermath of the relationship. Length: it should come to roughly 250-400 words.)

must_cover: Use the writer’s experience to explain why they believe the recipient is experiencing abuse; describe how hard being alone was after the breakup and how life gradually improved.
Explain why returning the key is insufficient and encourage changing the locks.
Encourage professional help and rebuilding personal connections.
Mention requesting police accompaniment for a property exchange when concerned about safety.
Express hope that the recipient becomes better able to recognise abuse and never experiences it again.
